construct: The greater petrosal nerve leaves the facial nerve near the geniculate ganglion and carries parasympathetic fibers for lacrimation. More distally, the mastoid segment gives off the nerve to stapedius and then the chorda tympani, which carries taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands. A lesion between the greater petrosal takeoff and the stapedius/chorda branches preserves lacrimation but causes ipsilateral lower-motor-neuron facial weakness, hyperacusis, and loss of anterior-tongue taste.

adversarial_second_pass.independent_reconstruction: Complete ipsilateral LMN facial weakness plus hyperacusis and anterior-tongue taste loss with preserved tears localizes the lesion distal to greater petrosal takeoff but proximal to stapedius and chorda tympani branches.
adversarial_second_pass.strongest_distractor_attack: A labyrinthine lesion proximal to the geniculate ganglion could produce facial weakness, taste loss, and hyperacusis, making it the strongest localization distractor, but it would also interrupt greater-petrosal lacrimal fibers.
adversarial_second_pass.expert_reviewer_reversal: Preserved lacrimation together with loss of stapedius and chorda functions uniquely places the lesion in the intratemporal facial nerve after the greater petrosal branch and before the later mastoid branches.
